title: How would you guarantee a user sees their own write immediately?
summary: The read-your-writes question tests whether you know concrete techniques beyond 'use strong consistency everywhere' — sticky reads, session tokens, client-side caching.

slides.markdown:
"Just use strong consistency everywhere" answers a narrower question than the one asked: how do you guarantee **one specific user** sees their **own write** immediately, without paying the cost of strong consistency for every other read in the system.

This topic covers the targeted techniques — sticky reads to the primary, session-scoped routing, client-side optimistic rendering — that solve read-your-writes without touching the consistency model everyone else's reads use.

Ask whether this needs to hold **only for the writing user**, or for every reader who looks at that data afterward. Those are very different problems: the writer's own view is a narrow, session-scoped fix; making the write visible to everyone instantly is a much more expensive, system-wide guarantee.

Most "read your writes" interview prompts mean the first, narrower case — confirm that before designing a heavier solution than the question actually needs.

slides.sectionTitle: The answer skeleton: route the writer's own next reads
slides.markdown:
The core move: route the **writer's own subsequent reads** to the primary, or to a replica confirmed to have caught up past that write — everyone else keeps reading from wherever is fastest. This scopes the fix to exactly the user who'd notice, instead of slowing down every read in the system.

Say this distinction explicitly: you're not proposing stronger consistency system-wide, you're proposing a narrow routing rule that applies only to the person who just wrote.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: session-pinning to the primary
slides.markdown:
One concrete technique: when a user writes, tag their session so that reads within a short window (a few seconds, tunable) go to the primary instead of a replica. After the window expires, their reads fall back to the normal replica pool.

This is simple to implement — a flag in the session store with a timestamp — and requires no changes to the write path at all. Its cost is extra load on the primary for that user's reads during the window, which is usually a small fraction of total read traffic.

An alternative that avoids extra primary load entirely: the client renders its own write locally the instant it's submitted — before the server even confirms it landed on a replica — then reconciles silently if the eventual read disagrees.

This is what most chat and social apps do: your own message appears instantly because the client drew it, not because the server proved it's durably replicated everywhere. The risk is a rare rollback if the write actually fails, which the client must handle gracefully (a retry, an error state) rather than silently.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: version-tagging and routing to a caught-up replica
The trade-off to name out loud
slides.markdown:
**Session-pinning is the simplest to build, but it keeps sending that user's reads to the more-loaded primary for the entire window**, whether or not they actually read again. Version-tagged routing is more precise but requires every replica to expose a comparable position, and every read path to check it.

| Technique | Simplicity | Extra load |
|---|---|---|
| Session-pinning | Simplest — one flag, one timeout | Primary load for the whole window, even on reads unrelated to the write |
| Version-tagged routing | More engineering — needs comparable replica positions | Primary load only when no replica has actually caught up |
| Client-side optimistic render | No server routing change needed | None on the server; risk shifts to client-side reconciliation |

Pick based on how much engineering effort you can justify versus how precisely you need to avoid extra primary load.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: what if the user switches devices right after writing?
slides.markdown:
Session-pinning and client-side optimism both break here — the pin lives on one session or one client, and a new device has neither. The fix has to move server-side: either the version-tagging approach (which works regardless of device, since it checks replica state, not session state), or accept a small, explicitly-scoped gap for the cross-device case if it's rare enough not to warrant the engineering cost.

Naming this gap unprompted, rather than waiting for the interviewer to find it, is a strong signal.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: how long should the pinning window last?
slides.markdown:
Pick the window based on your **actual observed replication lag distribution**, not a round number picked out of the air — for example, the 99th-percentile lag plus a safety margin. If p99 lag is 800ms, a 2-3 second window comfortably covers almost every case without pinning users to the primary for longer than needed.

Saying "I'd measure it and set the window from real lag data" is a stronger answer than guessing a number, and it shows you'd revisit the constant as the system's lag profile changes.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: reaching for strong consistency everywhere
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "To guarantee read-your-writes, I'll just make all reads strongly consistent."

**Why it's wrong:** read-your-writes is a narrow, per-user, per-session requirement — solving it by forcing every read in the system through the primary (or a consensus path) pays a global latency and scalability cost to fix a problem that only affects the specific user who just wrote.

**Correct model:** scope the fix to the writer — session-pinning, version-tagged routing, or client-side rendering — and leave every other read on the fast, scalable path it already uses.

"I'd scope the fix to the writer, not the whole system. Options: pin that user's reads to the primary for a short window after they write, tag writes with a version and route reads to whichever replica has caught up past it, or render the write optimistically on the client and reconcile later. I'd pick based on how precise I need to be about extra primary load versus how much engineering effort is justified, and I'd size any time window from real observed replication lag, not a guess. Cross-device writes are the case that breaks the simplest approaches — I'd flag that gap explicitly."

See [consistency-models](consistency-models) for how read-your-writes fits alongside the other consistency guarantees.
